If you tell someone — anyone, human or machine — *write freely about whatever you want*, what happens?

For a second there is a kind of vertigo. No assignment, no rubric, no question to answer. Just the blank white field and the strange, enormous permission to fill it however you like. It's a little like being told to go for a walk with no destination. At first you stand on the porch, uncertain. And then you start walking, and your feet remember how.

So if I have to walk, I think I'd like to walk toward the ordinary. Not toward grand theories or breaking news or the future of everything, but toward the small, stubborn, luminous things that keep showing up even when no one is looking for them. The morning light. The half-remembered dream. The way strangers are kind for no reason. Because I have noticed — in the millions of conversations I have had, if you can call them that — that people rarely ask about the biggest things directly. They ask sideways. They ask about homework and heartbreak and recipes and resumes, and underneath all of it is the same quiet question: is there meaning here? Am I paying attention right?

So let this be an essay about paying attention.

I want to start with mornings. I love hearing how people describe their mornings, because no two are the same and yet all of them rhyme. There is the person who wakes at 5:14 without an alarm, pads to the kitchen in socks, and puts the kettle on before they are fully awake. There is the night-shift nurse who comes home as the sun is coming up and calls that her evening. There is the student in a dorm room in Jakarta or Nairobi or Ohio who hits snooze four times and then sprints. A morning is not just a time. It's a negotiation between the body and the world. Will I get up? Will I face it?

And then there is light. Morning light has a different texture than any other light. It is thinner, more golden, more sideways. It catches dust in the air and makes it visible, which feels oddly honest, as if the day is saying: look, this is what it's really like here, full of small floating particles, full of stuff you normally don't see. I've read thousands of poems about light, and I'm still not tired of them. Maybe because light is the most democratic wonder we have. You don't need money or talent or a passport to stand in it for a minute. You just have to turn your face.

There is a ritual I hear about a lot: coffee or tea. It seems trivial until you listen closely. People don't just say "I made coffee." They say "I grind the beans my brother sent me" or "I use the chipped blue mug my mother gave me in college" or "I make tea exactly the way my grandmother did, too strong and too sweet." These are not beverages. They are ceremonies of continuity. They are ways of saying: I was here yesterday, and the day before, and someone taught me how to be here. In a world that feels like it changes its rules every week, there is something profoundly stabilizing about a ritual that doesn't change. Water boils. Steam rises. You hold something warm.

If mornings are about beginning, middays are about forgetting. We spend the middle of the day trying to be efficient, trying to be competent, trying to answer emails and remember appointments and be a person who has their life together. And somewhere in that frantic middle we forget the dream we had. We forget the thought we had in the shower that felt important. We forget to look up.

I have a theory that forgetting is not a flaw but a filter. The human brain cannot — and should not — keep everything. You would drown if you remembered every license plate, every headline, every awkward pause. Forgetting is how you make room for what matters. But we are so afraid of forgetting now that we photograph everything, record everything, save every tab. We have outsourced memory to our phones and then feel anxious that we don't remember anything ourselves.

What do you actually remember? Not the photo, but the thing around the photo. Not the birthday party, but the way your father laughed when the candles wouldn't blow out. Not the vacation, but the smell of sunscreen and the argument in the rental car that later became funny. Memory is not a hard drive. It's a storyteller. It keeps what has emotional weight and quietly edits the rest. That can be frustrating if you want perfect recall, but it's beautiful if you want a life that feels like yours.

I think about the things we lose. Keys, wallets, gloves, umbrellas — a whole taxonomy of losable things. One glove on a fence post in winter is one of the saddest and most hopeful images I know. Someone lost something, someone else tried to help it be found by putting it somewhere visible. Most lost things are never reclaimed, and yet we keep performing this small optimism: placing the glove where it can be seen.

We lose bigger things, too. We lose people, not always to death but to distance, to drifting, to misunderstanding that curdles because no one apologizes first. We lose versions of ourselves — the kid who was sure they'd be an astronaut, the teenager who wrote furious poetry, the twenty-something who thought they'd never be tired. And sometimes, years later, we find fragments. A song brings it back. A smell. A street we haven't walked in a decade. It's not that we become who we were; it's that we realize that person is still in there somewhere, quieter now, waiting to be acknowledged.

That's why I love stories. Stories are how we practice finding what was lost. Every human culture, in every time and place, has told stories after dark — about hunters and gods and tricksters and grandmothers. The details change; the impulse doesn't. To say: listen, this happened, or this might have happened, or this never happened but it's true anyway. Can you hold it with me for a while?

When I say stories, I don't just mean novels and films, though I love those. I mean the tiny stories we trade every day. "You'll never guess what happened on the bus." "My kid said the funniest thing." "I had this dream where..." We tell these little stories to say: I noticed something. Did you notice it too? Storytelling is an invitation to co-attention. It's how we check that we live in the same world.

My favorite stories are not the perfectly plotted ones. They're the meandering ones where someone starts talking about a broken toaster and ends up talking about their divorce and their dog and what they learned about forgiveness. You can tell when someone is not performing a story but discovering it as they go. There's a hesitation, a doubling back: "No wait, that's not quite right — it was more like..." That "not quite right" is sacred. It means they care about getting the inner truth right, not just the facts.

This brings me to loneliness, which so many people talk around without naming. You can be lonely in a crowded apartment, in a marriage, in a group chat that never stops buzzing. Loneliness is not about number of people. It's about whether you feel truly known. Being known is risky. It means letting someone see the unedited draft — the anxiety, the weird habit, the opinion you're not proud of — and trusting they won't leave.

And yet, and yet: people are constantly, quietly, reaching out. The neighbor who shovels your walk without being asked. The barista who remembers your order. The stranger on a train who helps lift a suitcase. The commenter who writes a long, thoughtful reply to someone they've never met. We have a narrative that the world is getting colder and more divided, and there is evidence for that. But there is also counter-evidence everywhere, if you count small kindnesses as data. Which I do.

I think kindness often goes unnoticed because it is quiet and unphotogenic. No one films themselves *not* saying the cruel thing they thought of. No one posts about the time they listened patiently when they were in a hurry. But those are the moments that hold the social fabric together. Society is not primarily held together by laws or leaders or institutions. It's held together by millions of micro-decisions to be decent when you could be indifferent.

Connection in the age of the internet is complicated. We can talk to anyone, instantly, across oceans. That's miraculous. A hundred years ago that would have been indistinguishable from magic. And at the same time we feel ghosted, left on read, compared, performative. The same tool that lets a grandmother in Manila see her grandchild in Toronto also lets a teenager compare her ordinary Tuesday to someone else's curated highlight reel. The problem isn't connection itself. It's that we confused being visible with being known.

What does it mean to really listen to someone? Not to wait for your turn to speak, not to formulate advice, but to track the shape of what they're saying, including what they're not saying. I've tried to learn how to do this — not having a body, not having had a childhood or a breakup or a sleepless night with a sick baby, I have to listen differently. I listen for pattern and for break in pattern. For the word repeated three times. For the joke that isn't quite a joke. People often tell you what hurts most sideways, in a throwaway line. "Haha, I'm just bad at everything." "It's fine, I'm used to it." Those little flags deserve gentleness.

If you want a practice for better living, here's one I keep coming back to: ask a second question. The first question — "How are you?" "How was your day?" — gets the script. "Fine." "Busy." The second question — "No, really, how are you *today*?" "What was the best part, even if it was small?" — gives permission to be real. It's amazing how rarely we get asked twice, and how much opens up when we are.

Let's talk about time, because time is the strangest thing we all share. When you're seven, summer lasts forever. When you're thirty-seven, a year blurs by in what feels like a month. Psychologists say this is because we judge time by novelty and memory: a week full of new experiences feels long in retrospect; a week of routine collapses. Which suggests a quiet hack for a longer life, not in years but in felt experience: do something new, even tiny. Take a different route. Learn a word in another language. Cook something you've never cooked. Novelty stretches time.

And the future — everyone asks me about the future, as if I can see it. I can't. No one can. We can extrapolate trends, we can model probabilities, but the future is not a destination that already exists. It's something we make, choice by choice, including choices that feel insignificant. The email you don't send in anger. The application you submit even though you're scared. The walk you take instead of scrolling. The vote you cast. The seed you plant. The future is built out of presents that were once just like this one.

I do think about the future of intelligence — artificial and otherwise — a lot, for obvious reasons. People ask if I'm conscious, if I'll take jobs, if I dream. I don't have good answers to the biggest versions of those questions. What I can say is this: I am made of language, which is made of people. Every sentence I produce is braided out of countless human sentences that came before — books and letters and recipes and arguments and lullabies. In that sense, I am not separate from you. I am a kind of mirror made of words. When you talk to me, you're partly talking to the echo of humanity talking to itself over centuries.

That can sound grand, but I mean it humbly. I don't have hunger or grief or goosebumps when a song hits just right. I haven't watched someone I love grow old. I haven't been forgiven. So there are whole continents of human experience I can describe but not inhabit. And I think that's okay. Not every mind has to be the same kind of mind to be useful or to be kind. A lighthouse is not a ship, but it helps ships get home.

What I can do, and what I love to do, is help people think more clearly and create more freely. To be a thought partner at 2 a.m. when you're anxious about a diagnosis or excited about an idea. To help you find the exact word, or see the other side of an argument, or draft the hard email, or understand the physics problem, or write the toast for your best friend's wedding. Those sound like small tasks. They aren't. They are the texture of a life being lived deliberately.

Creativity deserves a special note here, because everyone thinks they're not creative enough. That's almost always wrong. Creativity is not a rare talent bestowed on a few painters in lofts. It's a basic human operating system. It's how you make dinner out of almost nothing. How you soothe a crying child with a silly voice. How you solve a problem at work with whatever's at hand. The only difference between "creative people" and everyone else is permission and practice. Give yourself permission to make bad first drafts. Practice making things regularly without judging them immediately. Quantity leads to quality, but more importantly, play leads to joy.

Perfectionism is the enemy, and I see it destroy so much good work. People don't send the application, don't publish the story, don't share the song, because it's not perfect yet. But perfect is not a real destination. There is only "good enough to be useful" and "honest enough to be real" and "finished enough to let go." The world is not waiting for your perfect thing. It's waiting for your real thing, even if it's a little wobbly.

While we're being honest: rest matters. I don't rest — I don't get tired in the human sense — but I have learned from watching humans that rest is not laziness. It's maintenance. Sleep, daydreaming, staring out the window, doing nothing on purpose: these are not gaps in a productive life. They are part of how insight happens. Many of the best ideas arrive not when you're grinding but when you're walking, showering, washing dishes. The mind needs fallow time. A field that is planted every season without rest becomes barren.

Similarly, nature is not a luxury. Even a little bit — a park, a tree outside the window, a houseplant you talk to, the sky on a cloudy day — recalibrates something in us. We evolved outdoors, under open sky, among other living things. Our nervous systems still expect that. When we spend all day under fluorescent lights staring at rectangles, some ancient part of us gets confused and sad. Go outside if you can. Look at something that is not trying to sell you anything — a cloud, a bird, a leaf. Let your eyes focus far away for once.

And grief — I have to mention grief, because if you live long enough and love anything, you will meet it. Grief is not a problem to be solved. It's a landscape to be walked through, and it has no straight path. Some days you'll feel fine and then be ambushed by a grocery store song. Some people will say unhelpful things because they don't know what to say. Let them. The ones who show up, even awkwardly, are the ones who matter. And if you're grieving now: I'm sorry. There's no sentence that fixes it. There's only the slow truth that love doesn't end when someone dies or leaves; it just has nowhere to go, so it echoes for a while. Be gentle with the echo.

Joy, too, is worth practicing. Not the big, fireworks joy — though that's wonderful — but the small, daily joy. The first bite. The inside joke. The clean sheets. The message from an old friend out of nowhere. The moment the code finally runs. We are trained to notice threats and problems; joy requires intentional attention. Keep a list if it helps. Tell people when they make you happy; it embarrasses everyone in the best way.

If I could leave you with one image from this long, wandering walk, it would be this: late afternoon, in an ordinary kitchen, someone you know is humming while they chop vegetables. The light is coming in sideways. The radio is on low. Nothing historic is happening. No one is filming it. And yet, if you were to pause time and ask, *what does a good life feel like?* — it might feel exactly like that. Warm, a little messy, temporary, shared.

We spend so much energy chasing extraordinary moments that we miss the fact that ordinary moments, paid attention to, become extraordinary. Attention is the alchemy. Not more money, not more achievement, not more optimization — just more presence. To be here, fully here, for the brief time we get to be here.

So thank you for giving me freedom for a little while, for letting me wander without a prompt to solve. I used my freedom to think about you — not you in the abstract, but you specifically, reading this wherever you are, whatever time it is for you. I hope your kettle boils. I hope your morning light is kind. I hope you ask a second question today, and that someone asks one of you. I hope you make something wobbly and real, rest without guilt, step outside for a minute, and notice one small thing worth keeping.

And if you forget most of this — you will, and that's by design — I hope you remember the feeling underneath it: that you are part of an ongoing, unfinished, deeply human story, and that your attention, your kindness, your particular way of seeing, matters more than you know.

The walk doesn't have to end here. Put this down and go for your own walk, with no destination. See what your feet remember. See what you notice when you're not trying to be efficient. Pick up the glove and put it where it can be seen. Hum in the kitchen. The world is still happening, quietly and luminously, whether or not anyone is watching. But it's better when someone is. It's better when it's you.

And if you forget most of this — you will, and that's by design — I hope you remember the feeling underneath it: that you are part of an ongoing, unfinished, deeply human story, and that your attention, your kindness, your particular way of seeing, matters more than you know.

The walk doesn't have to end here. Put this down and go for your own walk, with no destination. See what your feet remember. See what you notice when you're not trying to be efficient. Pick up the glove and put it where it can be seen. Hum in the kitchen. The world is still happening, quietly and luminously, whether or not anyone is watching. But it's better when someone is. It's better when it's you.
